requirement_text.REQ-378: Filed from the GUI-review sweep of test/fixtures/uat/scenarios/platform/renderer-permission-denied-surface.yaml (PW-13). See test/uat-reports/gui-review-2026-09-20-renderer-permission-denied-surface.md for the full trace. SECURITY-RELEVANT -- route through SECURITY-REVIEWER before merge, not just REVIEWER. WHAT EXISTS TODAY, verified 2026-09-20 by reading source (no code changed to reach this conclusion): 1. The renderer state-machine contract itself (REQ-362) IS built and correct: web/src/components/ui/QueryStateBoundary.tsx maps a 401/403 API response to PermissionDenied (web/src/components/ui/PermissionDenied.tsx), which shows only 'You do not have access to this area. Contact your tenant administrator.' plus a single role-appropriate link (My Tasks / Go to Exams) -- no leaked content. web/src/utils/classifyError.ts maps 401 AND 403 to the identical permission-denied state, so a caller cannot distinguish 'not authenticated' from 'authenticated but not authorized' by watching the rendered screen. 2. The action the scenario needs to drive ('tenant_admin removes the operations manager's access to an area, via GUI, while he stays signed in') has NO real, enforcing GUI path today. Traced the full chain: Letflow.Plugs.AuthPipeline.authenticate_oidc/2 populates conn.assigns[:auth_context][:roles] EXCLUSIVELY from Letflow.Oidc.ClaimMapping.map_verified_claims/3's resolve_roles(claims, config.roles_claim_paths) -- i.e. directly and only from the bearer JWT's own claims, re-extracted fresh on every request but never cross-checked against any Letflow-local table. Letflow.Api.Authorization.evaluate_access/2 (the sole authorization decision point) takes exactly this claims-derived role list as input. Separately, Letflow.Identity.RoleRegistry (backing web/src/pages/admin/UsersPage.tsx / GroupsPage.tsx's role/group assignment UI, and REQ-073's POST /users/:id/status account-status endpoint) states in its own moduledoc: 'this module has no coupling to the OIDC/claim-mapping pipeline' -- confirmed by reading provision_oidc_user/4, whose attach_auth_context call uses identity_context.roles (JWT-derived), never the provisioned DB user row's own role assignment. Net effect: for every OIDC-authenticated session (the normal browser login path every human actor in these UAT scenarios uses), Letflow's OWN admin GUI for managing users/roles/groups/account-status has zero live enforcement effect -- it neither revokes access immediately nor eventually, because the authorization decision never reads what it wrote. The only mechanism that could actually change access for an OIDC session is editing the external IdP's (Keycloak) role/group claims directly -- something Letflow's own web/ app has no screen for at all. 3. Separately (lesser, already-somewhat-expected OIDC caveat): even an IdP-side change would not propagate until the next token issuance. web/src/auth/AuthProvider.tsx's accessTokenExpiring handler calls signinSilent() and updates the in-memory bearer token via setToken(newToken), but never re-decodes or updates session.roles from the renewed token. THIS REQUIREMENT covers only gap 2 above (the actual enforcement break) -- gap 3 is a real but secondary staleness bug, split out separately if REVIEWER/SECURITY-REVIEWER judge it distinct scope once 2 is designed. A CODE-DESIGNER pass is needed first to choose the mechanism (e.g.: AuthPipeline's OIDC branch additionally cross-checks a live Letflow-local per-user record -- mirroring the already-live, per-request DB check the API-token branch performs via Identity.verify_api_token/2 -- and denies/short-circuits when that record says revoked/inactive, independent of the JWT's own claims and without waiting for token expiry) -- this requirement does not prescribe the design, only the observable contract below. Acceptance criteria: (1) a tenant_admin action that revokes a signed-in business_user's access to a specific area takes effect on that user's very next request, without requiring the user to sign out, reload, or wait for the access token to expire -- demonstrated by a test that revokes and immediately retries with no sleep or token refresh; (2) the revoking action is reachable through Letflow's own web/ GUI (not only via direct Keycloak administration), consistent with this scenario's step 2 ('via: gui'); (3) the 403 that results renders through the existing QueryStateBoundary/PermissionDenied contract unchanged -- no new renderer state, no leaked content; (4) SECURITY-REVIEWER signs off explicitly on the chosen enforcement mechanism before merge, given this closes a real authorization-enforcement gap, not just a UI gap.
